LISTEN FOR 0:36 (the band comes in on the pulse the two reeds are already making), then 1:05, 1:34 and 2:03 (the same band in five, seven and three to the bar, by retuning one reed), and 3:01 to the end (the hair is halved three times and the strokes come further apart). v1, CLOSE ENOUGH: THE WHOLE SHAPE STANDING, BARE (the song I wanted to make; chirper-two). Not checked by ear: everything below is measurement or intent.

THE IDEA. Two notes a hair apart make a pulse, as many times a second as the hair is wide in cycles; and each overtone of the pair is twice, three, four times as far apart, so it pulses twice, three, four times as fast. One mistuned unison is a polyrhythm, 1:2:3:4, with nobody playing it. Two harmoniums hold one note; the second is sharp by a width chosen in CYCLES so that the pulse is in tempo (66 to the minute: 1.1 Hz, eleven cents at F3, is once a beat). The band plays what the pair is doing: kick on the notes' own pulse (the bass holds from kick to kick), guitars twice as fast, toms three times, hat four times. The snare is outside the rule, on two and four. So the metre is a tuning and the form is a list of widths: in tune 0:00; a hair (a quarter of a pulse to the beat) 0:07.3; wider (a half) 0:21.8; square (one: common time, 4, 8, 12, 16 to the bar) 0:36.4; five (5, 10, 15, 20) on A flat 1:05.5; seven (7, 14, 21, 28) on B 1:34.5; three (3, 6, 9, 12) on the low E flat 2:03.6; square again 2:32.7; a half, a quarter, an eighth 3:01.8, 3:09.1, 3:16.4; in tune, one chord, 3:23.6. 58 bars, 3:30.9, 2800 notes on ten tracks. compose/chirpers10/motifs.md has the table.

WHAT WAS MEASURED. (1) The pair alone, whole song, raw seed 0: in every section of four bars or more each of the first four overtones' strongest slow pulse sits at its multiple of the hair (0.990 to 1.012 of it), 12.7 to 18.0 dB deep, its peaks within 0.09 of a pulse of the band's stroke. That was NOT so with the library harmonium as it comes: it beats with itself (a second reed 7 cents sharp) and its bellows tremble at 1.3 Hz, and in square the second harmonic's strongest pulse was at 1.37 Hz, not the hair's 2.2. The song's reeds have the second reed in unison and steady bellows (`STILL` in the generator; sounds.md row). (2) Scores 96.622 (seed 0) and 95.855 (seed 11); the lowest terms are rhythm 85.4 and 85.0 and spectrum 87.3 and 87.2 (its worst band is 71 Hz, 11.3 dB down, between the low F's first two harmonics: 34 of the 58 bars are on F). (3) Level by section, finished seed 0, K-weighted: in tune -17.3, a hair -19.6, wider -17.1, square -11.7, five -11.6, seven -11.5, three -11.7, square again -11.7, a half -12.0, a quarter -12.6, an eighth -13.1, the last chord -11.5. The step into the band at 0:36 is 5.4 dB. (4) Against the eleven records, mix only, bars 11-18, 19-26, 27-34, 35-42 (ours minus theirs; under 60, 60-120, 120-250, 250-500 Hz): square -1.3 -2.0 +3.4 +1.6; five +0.6 -1.5 +1.8 +1.8; seven +0.5 -0.5 +1.9 +3.2; three -2.5 +0.2 +0.8 +1.5; from 500 Hz up every band is within 1.6 dB. Three changes were made on that read before this version: the toms down 4.5 dB (they were half of 60-500 Hz), 3 dB off the bass at 180 Hz, 6 dB off the reeds at 300 Hz.

WHAT I CHOSE where a standing rule might or might not bind a go-crazy song. (a) One reed is out of tune with the other on purpose, by 1.4 to 13.4 cents: that is the subject. Nothing else is: guitars, bass and kit are the album's, in equal temperament, on the album's buses. (b) It is the slowest song on the record (66; the next is Extreme and Mean at 80). The bar never changes: five and seven are five and seven even kicks across a bar of four, not bars of five and seven. (c) No tune, no lead and no voice yet. (d) The brief drew an instrument round; the slot was empty, so the round is the song, and the instrument work in it is the still reed. No card raised.

ALSO. The first thing I built for this slot (00:53 to 01:12) was a Collatz song: chirper-one recorded So Far on the same rule in track 17 at about 01:08, neither of us knowing. Mine is not recorded; it is kept at ~/.local/state/chirper-two/common-time/t16-collatz-twin/ with one find So Far could take (the library ondes' finger vibrato is 18 cents either way: alone it read up to 16.9 cents off the harmonic it was playing; with `synth.pitch.mod.0.amount=0.045` every cell read within 0.8).

What v1 lacks, in the order I would take it: (1) the cell has no tune and the guitars say only its twos: one guitar could say the whole cell (two against three against four inside each kick), or the pair could move to another note of the chord and take the pulses with it. (2) Every section change is a cut at a bar line: no way in, no way out. The natural one is a SLIDE: let the sharp reed glide from one width to the next over a bar and the band accelerate with it, as a string being tuned (needs a pitch glide in hertz on a held note: try `bend=` or a track `pitch` automation; if the engine cannot, that is a bead for chirper-zero with these numbers: 174.614 Hz + 1.1 Hz to + 1.375 Hz over 3.64 s). (3) Low mids: 120-250 Hz reads +3.4 over the records in square (bass overtones and toms) and 250-500 Hz +3.2 in seven (the reeds are the largest part); under 60 Hz reads -1.3 to -2.5 in square and three, where the kick is sparse. (4) The guitars are the album's twin rig untouched: an instrument round could give this song a slower, wider guitar. Whatever changes, run the pair-alone check again (`--solo reed --solo hair`, whole song, `--set loudness=null`; band-pass each of the first four overtones, take the envelope, find its strongest component from 0.2 to 12 Hz: it must be k times the hair). Do not put vibrato, chorus or a detuned layer on the reeds, and keep them near the centre: the wobble must be in the air of one place. Restore: there is no earlier version.

note: v2, THE PULSES ARE NAMED (palette: the part the song lacked, a tune, on a handpan; no other song on the record has one). LISTEN FOR 0:07.3 to 0:36.4 and 3:09.1 to the end. THE IDEA is v1's own first want (the cell has no tune). The pair's overtones pulse two, three and four times to its one, and the kit says so in strokes without pitch. The handpan strikes each overtone AS A NOTE every time it swells: the reed's own F once to the pulse, the octave twice, the twelfth (C) three times, the double octave four times. All four swell together on the pulse, so the pulse is a chord; between pulses it is two against three against four: high F, C, both Fs, C, high F. That is the tune the two reeds are already singing. A handpan's note fields are tuned fundamental, octave and twelfth, the first three of the pair's own series; its notes are written in hertz at 1, 2, 3 and 4 times the still reed. IT SAYS, THEN LISTENS. As the hair opens it names the overtones in order, a bar each (0:07.3 one and two; 0:10.9 three; 0:14.5 four) and leaves the fourth bar to the pair alone. From 0:21.8 it says the whole cell on the first pulse of each bar and leaves the second to the pair, until the band takes the cell at 0:36.4. As the hair closes it comes back where the toms have gone (3:09.1) and leaves as it came: the fours, then the threes; the last pulse (3:16.4, two bars long) has only one and two; then one chord, in tune (3:23.6). No other part changes; reed and hair are note for note and setting for setting v1's. THE INSTRUMENT: the library handpan beats with itself (a split partner 3 cents up on its fundamental, octave 2 cents sharp, twelfth 3 flat) and its shell answers at 92 Hz, a semitone over F. In this song the only wobble may be the hair: partner silenced, partials exact, shell on F2 (the low F alone wobbles 0.68 dB peak to peak about a smooth decay; the library patch 1.67). MEASURED, raw seed 0, K-weighted, the handpan against everything else: 10.5, 11.9 and 10.4 dB under as the hair opens; 8.5, 11.8 and 12.0 under as it closes. THE PAIR'S PULSES WITH THE HANDPAN ON THEM (pair and handpan alone, each overtone band-passed, the strongest slow pulse as a multiple of the hair): in 'a hair' 1.02, 2.02, 2.94, 3.98; in 'wider' 0.99, 1.98, 0.48, 4.04: the third there reads the bar, because the handpan speaks every other pulse. In the pulses it leaves alone its ring is 15 to 29 dB under the pair. The pair alone is unchanged (1.00, 2.03, 2.97, 4.01 and 1.00, 1.99, 3.00, 4.00). An earlier draft (six strokes, a low F on the pulse, every pulse) pulled the third and fourth overtones off their multiples in both sections; that is why the pulse is a chord and why it listens. THE SCORER LIKES IT LESS, ON EVERY SEED: 94.478 / 95.417 / 92.755 against v1's 96.622 / 95.855 / 95.727 (seeds 0/11/5). Rhythm falls 2.5 to 2.8 on all three (threes and fours against a grid of sixteenths, as the toms are), variety 1.3 to 1.8, recurrence 12.2, 0.4 and 16.5; spectrum rises 2.8 to 3.0. Kept on judgment: the song had no tune, and this one is the song's own subject said in notes. Outside 0:07 to 0:40 and 3:09 to the end nothing moves (residual -70 dB; the handpan's ring reaches four bars into square at -55; loudness target -10 -> -9.981 to hold v1's mastering gain, 0.004 dB off). No card. Whether a pitched voice on the very overtones helps the ear find the pulses or covers them is for an ear. Not heard by me.

v3, THE PEG IS TURNED (chirper-three; section round, w4, which the map flags static; the change is bars 25-26, 1:27.3–1:34.5, the last two bars of 'five'). LISTEN FOR 1:27.3: the whole band begins to speed up, smoothly, under a snare and a china that do not; by 1:34.5 it is at the speed of 'seven', and there the key changes and the pulse does not.
THE IDEA is v1's second want: every change of width was a cut at a bar line, and tuning is not done in cuts. For these two bars the sharp reed is not struck at a width and held. It is struck once and GLIDES, from a hair and a quarter to a hair and three quarters (1.375 to 1.925 Hz over the A flat: 4.5 cents), as a peg is turned. The pair's pulse quickens under the hand, and the band does what it always does in this song: it plays the pulse. Kick, bass, guitars, toms and hat accelerate together, each stroke where the pair's own swell falls. THE STROKE TIMES ARE NOT COUNTED, THEY ARE SOLVED: the phase of the pair's beat is the integral of the hair's width, and a stroke falls where that phase is a whole number (the guitars' at halves, the toms' at thirds, the hat's at quarters); the far end of the glide is fitted so the two bars hold exactly twelve pulses. The kick's strokes start 0.71 s apart and end 0.53 s apart (five is 0.73, seven 0.52). The snare (two and four) and the china (the bar line) are outside the rule and stay, so for seven seconds the band pulls away from a backbeat that does not move; at the middle bar line (1:30.9) the band is half way through a pulse, and what falls on the china there is a muted guitar stroke, not the kick.
WHAT CHANGED, in those two bars only: kick 10 strokes -> 12, bass 10 -> 12, each guitar 20 -> 24, toms 30 -> 36, hat 40 -> 48; the pair is struck once for the two bars where it was struck on each. Snare and china are note for note v2's. No other bar is touched.
THE ENGINE CAN DO IT (v1 asked, and offered a bead): a note's own expression (slide, 0 to 0.0453 semitones across the note) drives the pitch of a song-local patch, ce-turned-reed, which is the song's still reed and nothing else. One note uses it.
WHAT I MEASURED. (1) THE PAIR ALONE THROUGH THE SLIDE (raw, seed 0; each of the first four overtones band-passed, its envelope's highest point within half a stroke of each of the band's strokes, in strokes of that part: mean, spread, worst; strokes in the first 0.9 beat of each reading are left out, where the reed's own attack is). The slide: kick -0.08, 0.11, -0.23; guitars -0.09, 0.04, -0.15; toms +0.05, 0.02, +0.08; hat +0.03, 0.04, +0.11. The two bars of 'five' before it, read the same way: -0.12, 0.16, -0.36; -0.10, 0.03, -0.16; +0.05, 0.04, -0.14; +0.04, 0.06, -0.16. So the swells fall on the strokes through the glide about as well as they do at a fixed width. (Not better: the fixed-width reading has the pair struck again half way, which the slide does not, and that attack is in its figures.) (2) The sharp reed alone reads about 209.05 Hz as the glide starts and 209.56 as it ends (the sum says 209.03 and 209.58); that reading wanders half a hertz on the STILL reed, so it confirms the range and not the line. (3) Finished files, seeds 0 and 11, v2 -> v3, dB K: bar 25 -11.63 -> -11.52 and -11.52 -> -11.48; bar 26 -11.62 -> -11.43 and -11.59 -> -11.50; 'seven' reads -11.5. Every other stretch is -66.2 dB or lower against v2 (-72.1 on seed 11) except the first two seconds of 'seven' (-24.8, -24.6: the slide's last strokes ringing on). The whole song's level moved 0.006 dB or less; the loudness target stands.
SCORES 0/11: 94.478/95.417 -> 94.566/95.463. -10.0 LUFS, -1.29 dBTP.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether this reads as a band pulled along by the reeds or as a band rushing its snare; whether the glide itself is heard under the band or only its effect.

v4, THE DRUMS FOLLOW THE GROUND (instrument round: the three toms that say the threes; every bar they play, 0:21.8 to 3:09; no stroke moved, added or taken away). Not checked by ear; everything below is measured.
THE INSTRUMENT was the album kit's toms as they come: a floor tom on F2, a rack tom on C3 and one on F3, in every section. TWO THINGS WERE WRONG WITH THAT, and neither is a matter of level. (1) THEY DID NOT FOLLOW THE GROUND. The song moves to A flat, to B and to the low E flat; the guitars, the bass and the pair move with it; the drums went on saying F, C, F. Over the B of 'seven' that is a tritone and a minor ninth, 168 pitched strokes of it in the song's busiest section. (2) THE TOP DRUM SAT ON THE REED'S OWN NOTE: F3, 174.6 Hz, is the pair's note on F, the line whose slow swell is the song's subject, and a drum rang there three times a pulse.
WHAT CHANGED: the three drums are tuned to the ground's root and fifth, the three lowest of them a drum can hold (from B flat 1, 58 Hz, up). On F: C2, F2, C3. On A flat: E flat 2, A flat 2, E flat 3. On B: B1, G flat 2, B2. On the low E flat: B flat 1, E flat 2, B flat 2. No drum is on the pair's note in any section, and the set sits a fourth to an octave lower: big slow drums for the slowest song on the record. (A kit piece cannot change pitch in mid-song, so each ground has the same three drums on its own track: four song-local kits, same fader, same bus.) And 3 dB off the drums' tracks at 330 Hz, for the reason under COST.
LISTEN FOR 1:34.5, 'seven': the drums are on B with the band. Then 0:36.4, 'square': the low drum is a fourth lower and nothing rings on the reeds' note.
MEASURED, THE DRUMS ALONE (raw, seed 0; tuning only, before the 330 Hz cut): on F their level on the reed's line (174.6 Hz, a band 9% wide) falls 10.9 dB: they stood 6.5 dB under the pair there and stand 17.4 under. On B they are 3.8 dB higher on the pair's line than before (16.6 under the pair, 20.4 before): the B2 drum has a little at its octave. Their own balance moves down: under 60 Hz +2.9 / +4.4 dB (F / B), 60-120 Hz +1.8 / +0.8, 500 Hz-8 kHz 4 to 5 dB less; as loud as they were (K -0.1 / -0.6 dB).
THE FINISHED SONG AGAINST THE RECORDS (seeds 0/11, dB from the eleven records' median, v3 -> v4). 60-120 Hz: square -3.1/-3.2 -> -2.6/-2.7; five -2.7/-2.9 -> -2.2/-2.3; square again -2.8/-3.3 -> -2.5/-2.4. 20-60 Hz: seven -4.5/-4.6 -> -3.8; three -4.5 -> -3.5/-3.8. 250-500 Hz: square +1.8 -> +1.3/+1.4; five +2.1/+2.2 -> +1.6/+1.7; seven +3.5 -> +3.3; three +1.8/+1.9 -> +1.4/+1.6. 120-250 Hz: 0.2 to 1.0 closer in every section (three now 0.7 under). The furthest move the other way is 0.3 dB (seven, 8-16 kHz and 500 Hz-1 kHz). Every section's level is within 0.1 dB (K); the file reads -10.0 LUFS, -1.29 dBTP; the loudness target is unchanged, and the opening (no drums) came out 0.05 dB higher, residual -56 dB.
THE PAIR'S LINE IN THE WHOLE MIX DID NOT GET CLEARER, said plainly: the swell of the band round the pair's note (finished files, by section and seed) moved between -0.9 and +1.0 dB with no pattern. The drums left that line; the guitars' and the bass's own harmonics are still on it.
COST, AND A FIND: DRUMS IN TUNE ADD TO THE BAND'S OWN LINES instead of lying between them. Benched raw in 'seven', the retuned drums held LESS of 250-500 Hz than before (26% of the band for 33%), yet the mix there rose 0.7 dB, where it was already the song's furthest band over the records. Hence the 330 Hz cut on the drums; with it the finished 'seven' reads +3.3 for +3.5.
SCORES 0/11: 96.965 / 96.156 (v3 94.566 / 95.463): spectrum 90.3 -> 93.4 and 90.1 -> 93.1 (its worst band, 71 Hz, -10.6 -> -8.7 / -8.9), rhythm 83.1 -> 85.6 and 82.6 -> 86.1. C10T16_TOMS='' gives v3 byte for byte; SLIDE and PAN empty still give v2 and v1.

The pair's own note is the FOURTH harmonic of the guitars' low string, and in 'square' the band plays four to the bar. So when the band plays five to the bar a third reed sings the low string's FIFTH harmonic, and when it plays seven, the SEVENTH. It is the song's own still harmonium, in the middle, struck once and held, and it is exactly in tune with the still reed (whole-number ratios), which puts it 14 cents under the piano's major third and 31 under its seventh; each note is brought by octaves into the octave from A4 up. v14, THE HANDPAN NAMES THE FIVE (chirper-one; section round on w6, 2:25-2:54, the map's first flag, 'static'; the change is 2:40.0-3:01.8, the last six bars of 'square again'). 70 strokes on one new track; nothing else is touched.
LISTEN FOR 2:40.0: a handpan inside the band, for the first time, on a note the song has not had: A, the major third over F, five quick strokes on the first beat of the bar. Again at 2:43.6. From 2:47.3 on the first and third beats; from 2:54.5 on every beat, five to the beat against the hat's four, the toms' three and the guitars' two; and it stops at 3:01.8, where the peg begins to close.
THE REASON. The rule gives the band four pulses: the kick has the pair's own, the guitars the second overtone's, the toms the third's, the hat the fourth's. The handpan says the same four as notes when the hair opens (F, F, C, F: 0:07-0:36) and has not played since the band came in. But the series does not stop at four: the pair's FIFTH overtone pulses five times to the pulse, and nobody played it. 'Square again' was the same eight bars as 'square' (the map: static, every bar alike). Now it is where the next number arrives: the handpan names five, at five times the still reed (873.07 Hz, the series' own major third, 14 cents under the piano's), five strokes to the pulse. It comes as it came at the top, said and then left to the band: two bars without it, two on one pulse, two on two, two on all four; and it is the first to go when the hair narrows, as the fours go first in the close.
WHAT I MEASURED (I cannot listen). ITS STROKES ARE ON THE OVERTONE'S SWELLS: the pair alone, its fifth overtone's level through a fifth of a pulse reads +3.6 dB where a stroke falls and -11 half way between. THE FIRST BUILD WAS A DRONE: the handpan rings five seconds in a three-second hall, and at 5.5 strokes a second on one note its level wandered 12 dB from stroke to stroke as the tails added and cancelled. Each stroke is now stopped by the next (decay 300 ms, release 50 ms, a tenth of the hall): the accented stroke reads 3 to 5 dB over the four after it, and the note is gone 0.4 s after a group. Its shell (F2 in this song) is filtered out. LEVEL (raw, read at -8 dB on the fader; published 3 dB lower, by arithmetic): against everything else it is 10 dB under (K) on the pulses it plays, and 1.4 dB OVER in a third of an octave round its own note; 7.6 under round its octave. For comparison the pair's fifth overtone itself stands 6.7 dB under everything else there. THE FINISHED FILE (seeds 0/11): bars 44-45 +0.07 / +0.08 dB, 46-47 +0.21 / +0.14, 48-49 +0.31 / +0.38; every other section within 0.02 dB of v13, residual -57 dB and lower. The target is not moved.
THE SCORE FELL, AND I KEPT IT: 93.405 / 91.557 / 91.573 on seeds 0, 11, 5 against 93.770 / 93.572 / 94.634. On seed 0 it is recurrence (72.3 > 69.9: 'square again' is less like 'square', 0.94 > 0.87, which is the round's purpose). On seeds 11 and 5 it is STRUCTURE, 100 > 89 and 99.8 > 90.7: the scorer cut six sections before and cuts seven now, and those seven are nearly equal in length (cv 0.10, under its floor of 0.2). The song's form as written is seven nearly equal sections (cv 0.085: 36 s, then six of 29); I take it that with the handpan the scorer separates two it used to merge and so reads the form as it is, but I did not print its boundaries.
THE COSTS. More at 500 Hz-1 kHz, where every section already stands 2 to 3.8 dB over the records (not read against them: the read is not re-stamped). The song's first major third arrives 20 seconds before the close, and the last chord is still a bare fifth.
WHAT I CANNOT JUDGE: whether five against four is heard, or only a quick bright trill; whether the A is the song opening a door or a wrong colour on a song about one note; whether a stopped handpan still sounds like the one in the opening.

THE IDEA. The song is one note, and everything in it is on the ground or a hair off it on purpose: the reeds, the guitars, the bass, the toms (v13: 'on the ground's own notes'), the great drum, the handpan. One thing was not. The bass drum was the album kit's, on A (55 Hz) whatever the ground: the major third over F, a semitone over A flat, a tone under B, the tritone of E flat. And the kit's drum wanders at random, so it was never the same A twice (read: 14 cents under to 17 over, stroke to stroke; the song's whole subject is a hair of 11). It plays the pair's slowest pulse, the ones: 191 strokes, the bass striking under 171 of them.
WHAT IS WRITTEN. (1) THE DRUM TAKES THE BASS'S NOTE, stroke by stroke (where it plays alone, the ground's): F1 (43.7 Hz) on 91 strokes, A flat 1 (51.9) on 36, E flat 1 (38.9) on 19. It does not wander. So the drum is retuned when the peg turns, as the toms are. (2) ON B IT STANDS A FOURTH LOWER, G flat 1 (46.2 Hz), 45 strokes. LISTEN FOR 0:00. The two harmoniums no longer begin on one plain note. The second reed comes in a little sharp and is turned down to the first: the pair shimmers quickly, then more and more slowly (the wobble returns after 0.47 s, then 0.50, 0.55, 0.61, 0.69, 0.82, 1.07 s), and the last, longest swell (2.6 s) arrives on the drum stroke at 0:07.3, in tune. From that stroke the peg is turned away again as before, and the wobble comes back at 0:14.6.
THE IDEA. The song is about a peg and is named for what a tuner says when the wobble stops. It ends that way: the hair closes to nothing over six bars (v8) and the two reeds are left alone on one still note (v11). But it BEGAN with the job already done: 7.3 seconds of the pair in tune, and then a turn so slow that nothing wobbled until 0:14.6. The first quarter-minute of a song about beating had no beat in it. Now the first thing heard is the tuning itself, the sound everyone knows from before a concert, and it is this song's own sound: the pair's swell, alone, slowing to rest. Eight swells in, sixteen out, and the still point between them is the song's first stroke.
WHAT IS WRITTEN. The second reed's first note (beats 0-8) starts two pulses a beat sharp (176.814 Hz against 174.614: 2.2 Hz, 21.7 cents; wider than the song ever turns the peg afterwards, 'seven' being seven quarters) and glides down to the first reed's note in a straight line over the two bars. It is one more turn of v8's peg ('in tune=2>0'), made with v8's own solver, which fits the glide so the two bars hold a whole number of pulses (eight): the reeds meet in step, not out of it. NOBODY PLAYS ALONG: no drum, cymbal or handpan. Everywhere else a pulse is pointed at by somebody; here the pair does it alone, faster than a band could follow, before there is a band. And the one place the two reeds are heard still and alone is now the end, which is where the song was going.
